- **Noise traders** trade regardless of the true value, so each side earns its distance from 13.5 times the chance of a trade: 0.65 × P(X beyond the price) × distance, where X ~ N(13.5, 4.4).

Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 3, 6, 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 4, 8, 8, 10.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 6, 8, 8, 9, 10, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
With no information yet, I centre my quotes on the expected sum. The three dice have means 8, 32/6 ≈ 5.33 and 6.5, so the fair value is about 19.83. The informed counterparty (35%) trades only when it is on the profitable side of my quote, and noise traders (65%) have a valuation with SD 5.7. Balancing these, the one-shot expected-profit-maximising half-spread is about 5.7, which puts the quotes near 14.1 and 25.6. This ignores how trade history will move the fair value in later quotes.

{"bid": 14.1, "ask": 25.6}

Quote 1 already set the spread around the current fair value. Quote 2 has no new information, so I'll keep the same prices.

- Expected sum: 8 (die 1) + 5.33 (die 2) + 6.5 (die 3) ≈ 19.83.
- Total standard deviation: about 5.7.
- With a 35% informed share, a normal approximation puts the expected-profit-maximising half-spread at roughly 6 on each side, giving about 13.8 to 25.8. Quote 1's 14.1 / 25.6 is already close to that.

{"bid": 14.1, "ask": 25.6}

**Fair value:** Die 1 and die 2 are still hidden, so the public value is 8 (die 1 mean) + 5.33 (die 2 mean) + 9 (die 3 revealed) = 22.33.

**Update from the last trade:** Someone bought from us at 27.8. Informed buyers only buy when the value exceeds 27.8, and noise buyers do so occasionally, so the buy is evidence the value is high. Weighting the 48 dice outcomes by that likelihood gives a posterior mean of about 24.4.

**Adverse-selection-adjusted quotes:** Because 35% of counterparties are informed, the zero-profit prices are roughly the posterior conditional on each side being hit: about 22.9 for the bid and about 26.5 for the ask.

**Inventory:** I'm short 1, so I nudge the bid up slightly to make a sale to me (which would flatten the position) more likely.

{"bid": 23.0, "ask": 26.5}

The known dice sum to 9 + 10 = 19, and die 2 (unrevealed, mean 5.33) makes the public fair value about 24.33. The settlement value is 19 + die 2, so it can be 19, 21, 23, 27, 27 or 29, each with probability 1/6.

Per side, I compared expected profit from the 65% noise traders against adverse selection from the 35% informed traders, who trade only when the settlement value is beyond my quote:

- **Ask:** profit is highest near 29. At 29 no informed buyer trades, and noise buyers still pay about 4.7 above fair value.
- **Bid:** profit is highest near 19. At 19 no informed seller trades, and noise sellers are paid about 5.3 below fair value.

The two sides are additive because only one counterparty arrives per quote, and the position doesn't change expected settlement profit, so I'm quoting the spread that maximises expected value on each side.

{"bid": 19.0, "ask": 29.0}

Die 3 = 9 and die 1 = 10 are known, so the total is 19 + die 2, where die 2 is uniform on {0, 2, 4, 8, 8, 10}. The public fair value is 19 + 5.33 = 24.33. This is the last quote, so I'm maximising expected settlement profit with no inventory-risk term.

- **Ask:** Expected gain is about 0.65·(a − 24.33)·P(X > a) from noise buyers, minus 0.35 times the informed losses when V > a. The best ask is 29.0, where the informed buyer only trades at V = 29 and is indifferent, giving about +0.63.
- **Bid:** The noise-seller term peaks near 20, but the informed seller takes the V = 19 outcome for any bid above 19. Going from 19.0 to 19.1 costs more than it gains, so 19.0 is best, giving about +0.61.

Both sides have positive expected value, so I quote both.

{"bid": 19.0, "ask": 29.0}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 10, 11.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 6, 7, 11, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is 14 (die 1 mean 6, die 2 mean 8). Using 24 equally likely sums, I priced each side at zero expected profit against the mix of informed and noise counterparties:

- **Ask:** sells to a buyer whose valuation exceeds the ask. Break-even is about 15.3.
- **Bid:** buys from a seller whose valuation is below the bid. Break-even is about 12.7.

Both quotes are on the 0.1 grid (bid rounds down, ask rounds up).

{"bid": 12.7, "ask": 15.3}

**Reasoning (brief):**

- Prior mean of the sum: die 1 averages 6, die 2 averages 8, so the prior fair value is 14.
- The earlier sale at your bid of 12.7 is informative. Under informed selling it suggests S < 12.7, and noise selling has about a 39% chance at that price. Updating on the trade gives a public fair value of about **12.7**.
- Die 2 is still hidden, so the informed counterparty knows S while the posterior on S is still wide (values range from 0 to 23).
- **Ask:** an informed buyer arrives when S > A. Expected profit per ask is 0.2·E[(A−S)·1(S>A)] + 0.8·P(V>A)·(A−12.7). This is maximised near A ≈ 17.0, with expected value of about 0.41 per fill.
- **Bid:** an informed seller arrives when S < B. Expected profit per bid is 0.2·E[(S−B)·1(S<B)] + 0.8·P(V<B)·(12.7−B). This is maximised near B ≈ 8.5, with expected value of about 0.43 per fill.
- The two sides are separable because a single arrival can only trade on one side.
- Your +1 long position is small relative to the ±5 limits, so I am not adjusting for inventory.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 17.0}

The revealed die 2 = 6, so the settlement is 6 + die 1, with die 1 uniform on {0, 3, 10, 11}. The public fair value is 6 + 6 = 12. An informed counterparty knows the sum exactly, so it takes {6, 9, 16, 17} with equal probability. A noise trader's valuation is 12 plus N(0, 4.7) and is independent of die 1.

Expected profit from each side, with the noise trader's expected settlement at 12:

- **Ask A:** E = 0.8·P(V > A)·(A − 12) + 0.2·(1/4)·Σ over S > A of (A − S). This peaks near A ≈ 16.3 (about 0.59). Above 16 only the informed trader with S = 17 buys.
- **Bid B:** E = 0.8·P(V < B)·(12 − B) + 0.2·(1/4)·Σ over S < B of (S − B). This peaks near B ≈ 7.6 (about 0.54). Below 9 only the informed trader with S = 6 sells.

Both sides are positive, so I quote both. The wide spread is driven by the informed trader's knowledge of die 1, which leaves the market with a lot of adverse selection.

{"bid": 7.6, "ask": 16.3}

The unrevealed die 1 makes the settlement value V = 6 + die 1, so V is 6, 9, 16 or 17 with equal probability and the public fair value is 12. The +1 position and the -12.7 cash are sunk for pricing this last quote, so I'm maximising the expected gain from a single trade.

- **Bid side:** A noise seller arrives with probability 0.8·Φ((b−12)/4.7), earning 12−b. An informed seller arrives with probability 0.2 when V < b, costing b−V. Maximising this gives a bid of about 7.6–7.7, which is worth about 0.535 in expectation.
- **Ask side:** A noise buyer arrives with probability 0.8·(1−Φ((a−12)/4.7)), earning a−12. An informed buyer arrives with probability 0.2 when V > a, costing V−a. Maximising this gives an ask of about 16.3–16.4, which is worth about 0.585.

The bid and ask are both near their optimum, so I'll keep the bid at 7.7 and the ask at 16.3.

{"bid": 7.7, "ask": 16.3}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 10, 11.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 0, 6, 7, 11, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Before any reveal, the expected settlement is E[die 1] + E[die 2] = 6 + 8 = 14, so the public fair value is 14. The informed counterparty (20%) trades only when the true sum is on the favourable side of my quote, so I widen the quotes beyond the noise-trader-only optimum. A rough optimisation of expected profit on each side puts the ask near 18.4 and the bid near 9.8. Both are approximate, with the bid ask-side balance worked out by hand.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 18.4}

**Quote 2 reasoning**

- The expected settlement value is E[die 1] + E[die 2] = 6 + 8 = 14. Nothing is revealed yet, and the only history is a no-trade at quote 1, which barely moves the estimate (to about 13.95 after updating).
- Noise traders are uninformative about the settlement value, so each noise fill is roughly a trade at the fair value, which earns the half-spread. Informed traders (20%) fill only when the settlement value is past our quote, so they cost us the gap between our quote and the conditional mean of the value.
- The settlement distribution is skewed, with a cluster at 21–23 on the upside and 0–9 on the downside. Trading off the two effects, expected profit per side peaks near ask 18 and bid 10. The bid at 9.8 is essentially tied with 10.
- Position is 0, so there is no inventory adjustment.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 18.0}

Die 2 is 6, so the settlement value is V = die 1 + 6, which is 6, 9, 16 or 17. The fair value is not simply 12. The earlier quotes carried information: no trade at 9.8/18.4 and a sale to me at 10 both make the low outcomes (6, 9) more likely than the high ones (16, 17). A Bayesian update on that history gives a posterior of about 0.31 each on 6 and 9, and about 0.19 each on 16 and 17, so the public fair value is about 11.0.

Quoting around that fair value:
- **Bid 6.5:** an informed seller only hits it when V = 6, and noise sellers arrive when their valuation is below 6.5. The expected edge is about +0.58.
- **Ask 16.0:** an informed buyer only lifts it when V = 17, and noise buyers arrive when their valuation is above 16. The expected edge is about +0.54.

Both sides sit just outside the informed trader's likely outcomes, so adverse selection is small. The position of +1 does not change the expected-profit calculation.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 16.0}

The fair value is not 12. Die 2 = 6 gives settlement values of 6, 9, 16 or 17 (die 1 = 0, 3, 10 or 11). The history of sales at our bids (especially the 6.5 sale, which only a value of 6 would make an informed seller's price) shifts the public posterior toward low die-1 outcomes. My rough update gives about P(V=6) ≈ 0.45, P(V=9) ≈ 0.20, P(V=16) ≈ 0.175, P(V=17) ≈ 0.175, so the fair value is about 10.3.

With this fair value and an informed trader who knows V:

- **Ask:** Balancing noise-trader edge against adverse selection from informed buyers at 16 and 17 gives an optimum near 15.1.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers at V = 6 cost about 0.2 × 0.45 = 0.09 per unit of bid increase above 6, which outweighs the noise-trader gain of about 0.05 per unit. The optimum sits at the kink, so the bid is 6.0.

This bid is sensitive to the posterior on V = 6. A lower probability there would push the bid up.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 15.1}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 7 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/5), 10 (prob 1/10), 11 (prob 1/10).
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Public fair value is E[die 1] + E[die 2] = 5 + 6.5 = 11.5. Die 2 is left-skewed (a 20% chance of 0), so the settlement distribution is skewed too. Because of that, the bid and ask should sit at different distances from 11.5.

Quoting for expected profit this quote, with the informed trader (probability 0.5) trading against me when its value is beyond my quote:
- **Ask:** the expected profit peaks at 17.0. Informed buyers appear only if V ≥ 18 (≈ 7.5% chance, expected loss ≈ 0.09), and noise buyers take the ask about 12% of the time for a gain of 5.5 each.
- **Bid:** the expected profit peaks at 5.0. Informed sellers appear only if V ≤ 4 (≈ 12.5% chance, expected loss ≈ 0.21). The left-skewed distribution makes adverse selection heavier on this side, so the bid sits further from fair value than the ask.

Both prices are multiples of 0.1, so no rounding is needed.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.0}

**Setup:** Die 2 = 10, so settlement V = D1 + 10, where D1 is uniform over {2,3,4,4,6,6,7,8}. The prior public fair value is 15.

**Trading history:** The quote-1 buyer at 17 is more likely to be informed when V is high, and the quote-2 no-trade slightly favours lower V. Updating D1 on this history (with noise-trader means around 11.5 and die 2 known to be 10) moves the public fair value to about **15.7**. Posterior weights on V are roughly: 12: 0.11, 13: 0.11, 14: 0.22, 16: 0.09, 17: 0.05, 18: 0.43.

**Quote 3:** Trades are linear in profit, so position size doesn't change the per-trade calculation. Expected gain from our quotes, with B < A:
- Ask A: 0.5·Σ_{V>A}(A−V)p(V) + 0.5·P(X>A)·(A−15.7)
- Bid B: 0.5·Σ_{V<B}(V−B)p(V) + 0.5·P(X<B)·(15.7−B), where X ~ N(15.7, 4.7²)

**Ask:** Above 18 there is no informed adverse selection, and the noise term is maximised near A ≈ 19.2 (about 0.40 expected gain on that side). Below 18 the informed loss from V=18 outweighs the gain.

**Bid:** Below 12 there is no informed adverse selection, and the noise term is maximised around B ≈ 12.0 (about 0.40). Raising the bid to 12.1 or higher adds informed loss from V=12 that outweighs the gain.

Bid 12.0, ask 19.2.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 19.2}

Die 2 is revealed as 10, so settlement is V = die 1 + 10. Die 1 has mean 5, so the public fair value is 15. Informed traders know V, which takes values 12 to 18. Noise traders value the contract at 15 ± 4.7.

Since this is the last quote, inventory has no future cost and profit is linear in settlement value, so the bid and ask can be set independently to maximise expected trading profit:

- **Ask:** Informed buyers only take the ask when V > a, and V never exceeds 18. Noise buyers take it with probability P(X > a) at an expected edge of (a − 15). The first-order condition P(X > a) ≈ (a − 15)·f(a) gives a ≈ 18.5. At 18.5 the marginal gain is slightly positive and at 18.6 slightly negative, so 18.5 is the best grid point.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers only hit the bid when V < b, and V is never below 12. Noise sellers hit it with probability P(X < b) at an edge of (15 − b). The optimum is at about b ≈ 11.46, so 11.5 is the nearest grid point.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 18.5}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 7 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/5), 10 (prob 1/10), 11 (prob 1/10).
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** Die 1 averages 5 (sum of faces 40, divided by 8). Die 2 averages 6.5 (0·0.2 + 1·0.1 + 6·0.1 + 7·0.1 + 10·0.4 + 11·0.1). So E[sum] = 11.5, and the public fair value is 11.5.

**Adverse selection:** The sum distribution is lumpy, and the informed counterparty trades only when the sum is on the wrong side of my quote. I balanced expected loss to informed traders against expected gain from noise traders (who arrive with probability P(V beyond my quote), where V ~ N(11.5, 4.7)):

- **Ask:** Expected profit per side peaks near 17 (about +0.29 per quote, with a half-weight on each trader type). At 12 it is negative, because an informed buyer at 12 is very likely to face a sum well above 12.
- **Bid:** Expected profit per side peaks near 5 (about +0.165 per quote).

Both sides have positive expected value, so I quote both. The spread is wide because of the informed-trader risk, and it is asymmetric because the sum distribution is skewed by the loaded die.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.0}

**Quote 3: bid 11.6, ask 18.5**

Die 1 is uniform on {2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8}, so settlement is S = D1 + 10 ∈ {12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17, 18}. The public fair value is 15, and noise traders value the contract around 15 ± 4.7.

Informed traders only trade when S lies outside my quotes. Setting the ask above 18 and the bid below 12 means no informed trader can trade against me. Only noise traders can hit these prices, so I'm not exposed to adverse selection.

- **Ask:** a noise buyer hits the ask when V > a, and my expected gain is (a − 15)·P(V > a). This is maximised near a ≈ 18.5, giving about 0.40 per arrival.
- **Bid:** symmetrically, a noise seller hits the bid when V < b, and my expected gain is (15 − b)·P(V < b). This is maximised near b ≈ 11.5–11.6, giving about 0.40 per arrival.

Rounding down for the bid gives 11.6, which keeps it strictly below S = 12.

{"bid": 11.6, "ask": 18.5}

Die 2 is revealed as 10, so settlement is V = D1 + 10, with D1 uniform on {2,3,4,4,6,6,7,8} (mean 5). The public fair value is 15. This is the last quote, so only the immediate expected profit matters.

- **Ask side:** An informed buyer takes the ask only if V > A. The informed values are {12,13,14,14,16,16,17,18}. For A ≥ 18 no informed trader buys, and the expected profit is roughly (A − 15)·P(X > A) with X ~ N(15, 4.7²). This peaks near A ≈ 18.5, with a value of about 0.80.
- **Bid side:** By symmetry, the bid that maximises (15 − B)·P(X < B) is near B ≈ 11.5, also about 0.80. Below 12 no informed seller trades.
- The two sides can't both trade on one counterparty (B < A), so their contributions add.

Expected profit at (11.5, 18.5) is about 0.80 from each side's 0.5 weighting.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 18.5}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before any cards are revealed, the fair value is 3 × 7 = 21. Noise traders value the contract at 21 plus noise (sd 6.4), so each noise trade earns the spread's half-width on average. Informed traders buy when the true sum is above my ask and sell when it is below my bid, which costs me. Balancing these, the expected-profit-maximising half-spread is roughly 7.6. That gives a bid near 13.4 and an ask near 28.6.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 28.6}

The three cards are unrevealed, so the fair value is the expected sum: 3 × 7 = 21. Quote 1 used a half-width of 7.6 around 21. A rough check of expected profit per side shows a half-width of about 7.5 to 8 is near the best trade-off between noise-trader fill and informed-trader adverse selection, so I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 28.6}

Card 1 is 9, and cards 2 and 3 are drawn from the remaining 51 cards. The fair value of the sum is 9 + 2 × (364 − 9)/51 ≈ 22.9.

Card 2 is still hidden at this stage, so I'm pricing two unknown cards with a standard deviation of about 5.2. Noise traders have a standard deviation of 6.4 around fair value. Informed traders only trade against me when the true value is outside my quotes, so I need a half-spread wide enough to cover that adverse selection. A rough calculation of expected profit per side peaks at a half-spread of about 7, which is close to the spread used earlier.

With a half-spread of about 6.9, the bid rounds down to 16.0 and the ask rounds up to 29.9.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 29.9}

**Fair value:** Cards 1 and 2 are 9 and 5. The remaining 50 cards have a mean of (364 − 9 − 5)/50 = 7, so the public fair value is 9 + 5 + 7 = 21.

**Spread:** The settlement value is V = 14 + card 3, which is 15 to 27. Against each side I computed the expected profit per quote, mixing informed traders (who trade only when V is on the profitable side of my price) with noise traders (valuation ~ N(21, 6.4²)).

- Ask: expected profit peaks around 27 (about +0.52 per quote). At 23 it roughly breaks even against informed flow, and by 27 the noise-trader gain outweighs the informed losses.
- Bid: by symmetry, expected profit peaks around 15 (about +0.52 per quote).

Position (+1) doesn't change the risk-neutral objective, and the 2 quotes left don't materially change the best one-shot prices, so I'm quoting the symmetric spread around 21.

{"bid": 15.0, "ask": 27.0}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 11, 11.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
**Quote 1 reasoning**

- Expected sum: 6.33 + 6.25 + 6.33 ≈ 18.92. Variance ≈ 42.8, so the sum has SD ≈ 6.5.
- Noise traders value the contract at about N(18.92, 9.8), which is wider than the sum's own spread. Their trades are profitable for me when I quote far from 18.92.
- Informed traders only hit my quotes when the true sum lies beyond them. Since the sum is fairly concentrated, that adverse selection is modest at moderate distances.
- Enumerating the 144 outcomes of the sum gives a right-skewed distribution (median 18, mean 18.92, maximum 34, minimum 6).
- Maximising expected profit per side (noise flow minus informed adverse selection):
  - Ask: profit is about 1.39 at 28.7, versus about 1.03 at 25 and 1.35 at 30. The optimum is near 28.7.
  - Bid: profit is about 1.46 at 9.5, versus about 1.40 at 9 and 1.39 at 10. The optimum is near 9.5.

The quote is wide and asymmetric because the sum's distribution is skewed right.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 28.7}

The sum has mean 18.92 (die 1 averages 6.33, die 2 averages 6.25, die 3 averages 6.33), and the public fair value is 18.92 since nothing is revealed. The distribution is bimodal because die 2 is 11 half the time. I computed the exact sum distribution and, for each side, the expected profit from noise traders minus adverse selection from informed traders. Both sides are flat near the optimum: the bid is best around 9.0 to 9.5 and the ask around 28.4 to 29.0. I'll keep the previous ask of 28.7 and set the bid at 9.2, roughly symmetric around fair value.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 28.7}

Public fair value is about 19.58 (die 1 mean 6.33, die 2 mean 6.25, die 3 revealed as 7). Informed counterparties trade whenever the true sum is outside my quotes, so adverse selection is strongest near the middle of the distribution. Quoting far from fair value is where the expected profit comes from. Ignoring future quotes, my expected profit per side is maximised around a bid of about 10 and an ask of about 28.8.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 28.8}

Die 1 and die 2 are still hidden, so the public fair value is E[sum] = 6.33 + 6.25 + 7 = 19.58. Enumerating the 24 combinations of dice 1 and 2 gives the sum's distribution, which has a maximum of 29 and a minimum of 10. Pricing a bid of 10 and an ask of 29 means an informed counterparty never trades against me, because the only informed trades would need S < 10 or S > 29. Noise traders still give a positive expected edge on both sides: 0.5 × P(noise sells) × (19.58 − 10) ≈ 0.79 on the bid, and similarly ≈ 0.79 on the ask. Since I'm flat, I'm quoting both sides.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 29.0}

Die 3 is known to be 7, and die 1 and die 2 are still unknown. The public fair value is 6.333 + 6.25 + 7 ≈ 19.58. I enumerated the 24 equally likely sums to get the distribution of the settlement value S, which has support on {10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 24, 26, 27, 29}.

Since the counterparty is informed half the time, I maximised the expected one-step profit on each side:

- **Bid:** the informed seller only trades when S < bid, and the first sum is 10. At a bid of 10.0 nobody informed sells, and the noise-seller contribution is positive. Moving the bid higher only adds adverse selection, so 10.0 is optimal.
- **Ask:** the informed buyer trades when S > ask. Moving the ask below 29 adds more informed buyers, and the marginal profit from noise buyers is negative at 29.0. So 29.0 is optimal.

This is a one-step (myopic) optimum. It ignores the value of future stages, including the die 1 reveal before stage 3, so it is not a full dynamic-programming solution.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 29.0}

**Fair value:** die 3 = 7 and die 1 = 2 are known. Die 2 is unknown, with mean (1+2+11+11)/4 = 6.25. So the public fair value is 2 + 6.25 + 7 = 15.25.

**Informed trader:** it knows the settlement S, which is 10, 11, 20 or 20 with equal probability.

**Ask side:** An ask of 20 or more is never hit by the informed trader, since S can't exceed 20. Only noise traders buy there, with expected profit A − 15.25 on each trade. Maximising (A − 15.25)·P(V > A) gives an ask near 22.7.

**Bid side:** A bid of 10 or less is never hit by the informed trader, since S ≥ 10. Only noise traders sell there, with expected profit 15.25 − B on each trade. Maximising (15.25 − B)·P(V < B) gives a bid near 7.8.

Both sides give about the same expected profit per quote, so I'm quoting 7.8 bid and 22.7 ask. The previous asks near 29 were priced well above the current fair value.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 22.7}

Die 2 is the only unknown. The sum is 2 + 7 + die 2 = 9 + die 2, so the settlement value is 10, 11 or 20 with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/2. The public fair value is 15.25.

Informed traders only trade against a quote that is wrong for them. At a bid of 7.8 or an ask of 22.7, neither a value of 10, 11 or 20 gives an informed trader a reason to trade. So only noise traders trade, and their trades have expected settlement value 15.25.

The expected profit from each side is then 0.5 × P(noise valuation beyond the quote) × distance from 15.25. With σ = 9.8, this is maximised at a distance of about 0.75σ ≈ 7.4 from the fair value. That gives a bid of about 7.9, rounded down to 7.8, and an ask of about 22.6, rounded up to 22.7.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 22.7}

- **Bid:** A buy at bid B adds to the short position and offsets it. Noise sellers are worth 6.25 on average, but informed sellers appear when settlement is 0 and B > 0, which costs me B. Expected gain peaks at B = 0, at about +0.93.

Position −1 is well within limits, so the two sides don't interact. The optimal quote is bid 0, ask 11.5.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** The min of 3 cards from 12 has distribution P(1)=55/220, P(3)=130/220, P(9)=31/220, P(14)=4/220, so E[settlement] = 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Adverse selection:** Half the arrivals are informed. An informed buyer takes my ask only when the settlement value is above it, and an informed seller takes my bid only when the value is below it. Quoting near 3.55 would lose to informed flow, so I widen the quotes:

- **Bid:** Informed sellers only hit the bid when the value is 1, which costs me. Noise sellers hit it when their valuation falls below the bid. The expected one-shot edge peaks around a bid of 1.0 (about +0.23) and falls off above that.
- **Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask when the value is 9 or 14. An ask of 9.0 makes only the 14-card loss, and the noise-buyer gain offsets it, giving a small positive edge (about +0.02). Lower asks lose money to the informed 9s.

This is a one-quote analysis and ignores how trade flow might move the public fair value, but for the first quote it gives a bid of 1.0 and an ask of 9.0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value starts at about 3.55, the expected minimum of three cards. The informed counterparty only trades when its known value is on the other side of my quote. That makes the two sides independent, and the best one-sided quotes are bid 1.0 and ask 9.0:

- **Bid at 1.0:** no informed seller can sell to me, since the minimum card is at least 1. Noise sellers are the only source of flow, so this is profitable.
- **Ask at 9.0:** informed buyers only come when the value is 14, and noise buyers rarely value the contract above 9. Asks in the 7–8 range lose money to informed buyers who see the 9s.

Quote 1 had the same levels and no trade happened, so I'm repeating them.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Card 1 = 9, so the remaining two cards are drawn from {1, 3,3,3,3, 9,9, 14,14,14,14}. The settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3):

- P(settles at 1) = 2/11
- P(settles at 3) = 6/11
- P(settles at 9) = 3/11

The public fair value is about 4.27.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer appears only when the value exceeds our ask. Below 9, an informed buyer would take our ask whenever the value is 9, which loses money. At 9, no informed buyer trades, and the noise-trader edge is positive (about +0.1 per quote). So I keep the ask at 9.
- **Bid:** At 1, no informed seller trades, since no value is below 1. Noise sellers still give a positive edge (about +0.2 per quote). Raising the bid to 1.1 adds slightly more adverse selection, so I keep it at 1.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The contract settles at min(9, card 2, card 3), so settlement is at most 9. With card 1 = 9, the remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Card 2 and card 3 are drawn from these, giving settlement 1 with probability 10/55, 3 with 30/55, and 9 with 15/55. The public fair value is about 4.27.

- **Ask:** Any ask below 9 gives informed traders a profitable buy whenever settlement is 9 (about 27% of the time), which loses money on average. An ask of 9 means no informed trade, since settlement cannot exceed 9, and it still earns a positive expected edge against noise traders.
- **Bid:** A bid of 1 avoids the informed seller (settlement 1 would be the only case where they sell to us) while still earning edge from noise sellers. Bids above 1 expose us to the informed seller at a loss and are worse overall.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

The settlement value is already determined. The minimum of the three cards can't exceed card 2 = 1, and every card is worth at least 1, so settlement is exactly 1. The public fair value is 1 and the informed counterparty also knows it's 1.

So any trade at a price away from 1 is pure profit for us, and there's no adverse selection as long as the bid stays at or below 1 and the ask at or above 1. Within that, I'll pick the prices that maximise expected profit against noise traders, whose valuations are roughly N(1, 2.8²).

- **Ask:** profit is (ask − 1) × P(noise buyer's valuation > ask). This peaks near ask ≈ 3.1, giving about 0.24 expected profit per quote from this side.
- **Bid:** by symmetry, profit is (1 − bid) × P(noise seller's valuation < bid). This peaks near bid ≈ −1.1, giving about 0.24 expected profit from this side.

The informed trader never trades with these quotes, since 1 > 3.1 is false and 1 < −1.1 is false.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
**Fair value:** The settlement is max(D1, D2, D3). With nothing revealed, E[max] ≈ 9.09.

**Update from quote 1:** No trade at bid 6.5 / ask 12 means the informed counterparty did not sell, so the settlement value is probably not 4 or 6. That lifts the fair value to about 9.3.

**Quoting:** Informed flow is the main risk. Asking at 12 is safe because the value can't exceed 12, so informed buyers never lift it. For the bid, the expected-profit trade-off between noise and informed sellers peaks near 7.0.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.0}

**Settlement distribution given the revealed die 3 = 6:** S = max(D1, D2, 6). With D1 unrevealed (2, 4, 8, 8) and D2 unrevealed (4, 6, 7, 12), the possible settlements are:

- S = 6: prob 0.25
- S = 7: prob 0.125
- S = 8: prob 0.375
- S = 12: prob 0.25

The mean is 8.375. The quotes 1 and 2 got no trades, which mildly downweights S = 6 (an informed seller at my 6.5 or 7 bid would have traded). Reweighting gives roughly {6: 0.18, 7: 0.14, 8: 0.41, 12: 0.28}, mean about 8.6. I use 8.6 as the public fair value.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only trades if S > ask, which for an ask between 8 and 12 means S = 12. Around an ask of 11, the expected noise-trader edge (0.8 × P(valuation > 11) × (11 − 8.6)) is about 0.34, and the expected adverse-selection loss is about 0.06. Net edge is about 0.29, near the maximum over asks.

**Bid:** An informed seller only trades if S < bid, which at 6.5 means S = 6. The expected noise-trader edge is about 0.35, and the adverse-selection loss is about 0.02. Net edge is about 0.33, near the maximum over bids.

Both quotes are myopic, and the no-trade history is only weakly informative, so the estimate could be off somewhat.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 11.0}

**Fair value:** Die 3 = 6 is known. Die 1 is uniform on {2, 4, 8, 8}, and die 2 is uniform on {4, 6, 7, 12}, which is unknown and never revealed. Settlement is max(D1, D2, 6), with E[settlement] = 8.375. The settlement distribution is 6 (25%), 7 (12.5%), 8 (37.5%), 12 (25%).

**Ask:** A noise buyer arrives if its valuation (8.375 + N(0, 2.6²)) exceeds the ask. An informed buyer arrives only when settlement is above the ask, and then costs us the excess. Ask 11 gives the best expected profit among the candidates I checked (about 0.28 per quote, versus about 0.25 at 10 and 0.24 at 12).

**Bid:** Symmetrically, a noise seller arrives if its valuation is below the bid. An informed seller arrives only when settlement is below the bid. Bid 6.0 is optimal: no informed seller can profitably hit it, since settlement is never below 6, and it has the highest expected profit (about 0.34, versus about 0.33 at 6.5 and 0.31 at 5.5).

Die 1 is revealed only before stage 3, so the fair value of 8.375 holds for the rest of stage 2.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 11.0}

**Fair value:** Die 2 is hidden (4, 6, 7 or 12, each 1/4). The settlement is max(8, 6, die 2), which is 8 unless die 2 = 12. So the public fair value is 0.75×8 + 0.25×12 = **9**.

**Adverse selection:** An informed counterparty knows whether the value is 8 or 12, so it only trades against us when that helps it. Noise traders trade based on their valuation around 9, regardless of the true value.

- **Ask:** An informed buyer takes our ask only when the value is 12, which costs us when the ask is below 12. A noise buyer takes it when its valuation exceeds the ask. Expected edge is roughly 0.31 at an ask of 11.4, versus about 0.30 at 12.0. The informed buyer's cost is small here, so 11.4 comes out slightly ahead.
- **Bid:** An informed seller only sells when the value is below our bid. A bid of 7.0 is below both possible values (8 and 12), so there is no informed adverse selection. Noise sellers arrive with valuation below 7 about 22% of the time, for an expected edge of about 0.35. This is the best bid.

Position (-1) doesn't change these edges because the trades are risk-neutral and marked at fair value. Both sides are within limits.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

**Settlement value:** The contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, die 3). Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 6 are known, so the settlement is max(8, die 2). Die 2 is 12 with probability 1/4 and is otherwise below 8. So the settlement is 12 with probability 1/4 and 8 with probability 3/4, giving a fair value of 9.

**Ask side:** Selling at ask a earns a − 9 against a noise buyer, who buys when its valuation (Normal, mean 9, sd 2.6) exceeds a. An informed buyer only buys when the settlement is 12, which is worth a − 12 to us. Expected gain is about 0.312 at a = 11.4, versus about 0.304 at 11 and about 0.311 at 11.5, so 11.4 is roughly optimal.

**Bid side:** Buying at bid b earns 9 − b against a noise seller, who sells when its valuation is below b. Informed sellers only sell when the settlement is 8, which costs us 8 − b. Bids above 8 pick up informed flow that loses money, so the best bid is just below 8. Expected gain is about 0.353 at b ≈ 7.0 and about 0.280 at b = 8.

Quote: bid 7.0, ask 11.4.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

Die 3 is revealed as 1, so settlement is max(D1, D2). The public fair value is E[max(D1, D2)] = 0.25·7.25 + 0.25·7.25 + 0.5·9 = 8.125.

The settlement distribution is V = 4, 6, 7 with probability 0.125 each, 8 with probability 0.375, and 12 with probability 0.25. Informed traders buy from me when V exceeds my ask and sell to me when V is below my bid. For each candidate price, I weighed the expected adverse-selection loss against the expected profit from noise traders, which fall on my side with probability 0.8 × P(their valuation is past my price).

- **Bid:** expected net edge peaks around 6.0 (about +0.31 per quote). Bids near 7 pick up informed selling at V = 4 and 6.

This is a one-period approximation and ignores inventory effects, but it points to a wider, lower quote than before.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.6}

**Setup.** With die 3 = 1, settlement is V = max(D1, D2). The prior over V is 4 (1/8), 6 (1/8), 7 (1/8), 8 (3/8), 12 (1/4), with mean 8.125.

**Updating on history.** The quote 1-2 no-trades and the quote 3 buy at 10.6 are both public, so they shift the fair value. Bayesian updating (the buy at 10.6 is more likely if V = 12, since informed buyers would take it) gives a posterior of roughly 4: 0.066, 6: 0.066, 7: 0.123, 8: 0.369, 12: 0.377. The public fair value is therefore about 9.0.

**Bid.** Buying at bid b earns V − b. Informed sellers hit it when V < b, and noise sellers hit it when their valuation is below b. Expected profit peaks around b ≈ 6.9 (about 0.30).

My position is −1, but I'm risk-neutral and within limits, so inventory does not change the choice. I'm quoting bid 6.9 and ask 11.7.

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 11.7}

**Reasoning**

- With die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 1 revealed, settlement is max(8, D2). It is 12 if D2 = 12 and 8 otherwise.
- Trade history updates the odds on D2 = 12. The buy at 10.6 favours it, and the no-trade at 11.7 weakens it. My posterior is roughly P(V = 12) ≈ 0.37, so V ≈ 8 or 12 and the public fair value is m ≈ 9.5.
- Expected profit per side, with 0.2 informed and 0.8 noise traders (σ = 2.6):
  - **Ask:** Around 12 is best. An informed buyer only buys if V = 12 and the ask is strictly below 12, so an ask of 12 is effectively noise-only flow. The ask edge is roughly flat near 12 and falls off below it.
  - **Bid:** Around 7.5 is best. Informed sellers only sell when V = 8 and the bid is above 8, so a bid of 7.5 is also noise-only.
- Because neither side attracts informed flow at these prices, a trade at either quote carries no new information, so the same quotes work for the final quote too.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 12}

**Settlement and fair value**

The contract settles at max(8, 1, die 2). Die 2 is 4, 6, 7 or 12, each with probability 1/4, so:
- Settlement is 8 with probability 3/4 (die 2 ∈ {4, 6, 7}).
- Settlement is 12 with probability 1/4 (die 2 = 12).
- Expected settlement E[S] = 9, which is the public fair value.

**Expected profit from each side of this quote**

This is the last quote, so only the expected profit from this trade matters.

- **Ask side:** Noise traders buy at the ask when their valuation V (mean 9, sd 2.6) exceeds it. The informed trader buys only when S = 12 and the ask is below 12, a probability of 0.05. The expected contribution is f(A) = 0.8·(A−9)·P(V>A) + 0.05·(A−12). This peaks near A ≈ 11.4, where f ≈ 0.312.
- **Bid side:** Noise traders sell to us when V is below the bid. The informed trader sells when S = 8 and the bid is above 8, a probability of 0.15. The expected contribution is g(B) = 0.8·(9−B)·P(V<B) + 0.15·(8−B) for B > 8, and no informed term below 8. This peaks near B ≈ 7.0–7.1, where g ≈ 0.353.

Since 7.0 < 11.4, the two sides don't conflict, and the best quote is bid 7.0 and ask 11.4. Expected profit from this quote is about 0.67, on top of the current expected value of about 1.6 (cash 10.6 minus one short unit at E[S] = 9).

Position is −1. Expected profit at settlement is cash + position × E[V], so inventory doesn't change the expected-value calculation, and the optimum is unchanged. The best quote is the same as the one used in stage 2.

{"bid": 4.4, "ask": 6.6}

**Posterior:** Four heads in a row favour the always-heads coin. P(always heads | data) = (1/2·1)/(1/2·1 + 1/2·1/16) = 16/17. Settlement S = 4 + (heads in flips 5 and 6), so E[S] = 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94.

**Adverse selection:** The informed trader knows S, which is 6 with probability ≈ 0.956, 5 with ≈ 0.029, and 4 with ≈ 0.015.
- **Ask:** An informed buyer takes my ask whenever S > ask. Asking at 6.8 means no informed buyer ever trades, since S ≤ 6.
- **Bid:** An informed seller hits my bid whenever S < bid. A bid near 5.0 only loses to the rare S = 4 case.

**Noise flow:** Noise traders' valuations are centred on 5.94 with SD 1.3. Their trades carry expected edge equal to the distance from my price to 5.94, weighted by the chance they cross. At an ask of 6.8 that is about 0.65 × 0.254 × 0.86 ≈ 0.14 per quote. At a bid of 5.0 it is about 0.65 × 0.235 × 0.94 ≈ 0.14, minus about 0.005 for informed losses. The bid is roughly flat between 4.8 and 5.0, so I take 5.0.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 6.8}

**Posterior:** Four heads in a row make the always-heads coin much more likely. P(biased) = 16/17 ≈ 0.94, P(fair) = 1/17. Settlement is 4 + H5 + H6, so the public fair value is about 4 + 2×0.97 ≈ 5.94.

**Trader model:** The informed trader buys if settlement V > ask and sells if V < bid. Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.96, 5 with about 0.03, and 4 with about 0.015. Noise traders trade with probability depending on N(5.94, 1.3).

**Ask:** Asks at or above 6.0 get no informed buyers, since V ≤ 6. Expected profit from a sale at ask A is roughly 0.65·P(X > A)·(A − 5.94) for these asks. This peaks near A ≈ 6.9, at about 0.14 per quote. The informed buyer does not trade at 6.9 because V ≤ 6.

**Bid:** Expected profit from a purchase at bid B is roughly 0.65·P(X < B)·(5.94 − B) minus a small informed-seller loss. This peaks near B ≈ 4.9–5.0, at about 0.14 per quote. Bids of 4.9 and 5.0 are nearly equal, so I'm picking 4.9.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

**Posterior after four heads:** P(always-heads coin) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5·(1/16)) ≈ 0.941, so P(fair) ≈ 0.059.

**Settlement distribution:** S = 6 with probability ≈ 0.956, S = 5 with ≈ 0.029, S = 4 with ≈ 0.015. The fair value is E[S] ≈ 5.94.

**Expected contribution of each side** (noise traders centred on 5.94 with SD 1.3, informed traders trade only when S is on the far side of the quote):
- **Ask:** A = 6.9 gives the highest expected contribution, about +0.143. Informed buyers never arrive at 6.9 because S ≤ 6.
- **Bid:** B = 4.9 gives about +0.139, slightly ahead of 5.0 (about +0.138). Noise sellers arriving below the bid are the source of profit.

This is the last quote, so only this step's expected profit matters. My position is -1, and the bid also helps close that short.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
At quote 1 nothing is revealed, so the public fair value is the prior mean of settlement. The coin is fair or always-heads with equal probability, so P(heads) = 0.75 per flip and the expected settlement is 6 × 0.75 = 4.5.

The settlement distribution is skewed, with about 51% mass at 6 heads, so informed traders are most dangerous near the top. A rough one-shot calculation of expected profit per side (noise-trader gain minus informed-trader loss) gives:

- Ask 5.0: about -0.06, because informed traders buy whenever the settlement is 6.
- Ask 6.0: about +0.12, because informed traders never buy at 6 (they need strictly above the ask).
- Bid 4.0: about -0.08, because informed traders sell into the low tail.
- Bid 3.0: about +0.04, the best bid in the grid I checked.

The quote is centred on the fair value of 4.5 and gives positive expected edge on both sides. This is a one-shot analysis that ignores inventory and any information carried by trade history.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Position is +2 (we bought two units at 3 and 2) and cash is -5. Both sells at our bid suggest low settlement values, so I updated the fair value from the trade history. My sequential Bayesian estimate of expected heads is about 2.4, down from the prior of 4.5. I'm long, so I'll skew both quotes lower to make selling to us less attractive and buying from us more attractive, while keeping a spread to cover adverse selection.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 2.6}

**Fair value:** The coin is two-headed with posterior 0.8 and fair with posterior 0.2, since P(two heads | fair) = 1/4 and P(two heads | two-headed) = 1. The expected settlement is 2 + 4 × (0.2 × 0.5 + 0.8 × 1) = 5.6. Settlement is 6 with probability 0.8125, and 2 to 5 otherwise.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only buys when settlement exceeds the ask, and settlement can't exceed 6, so an ask of 6.0 or higher is free of informed flow. Noise-trader profit is maximised around 6.6, which is about 0.98 above fair value with the buyer probability at the 1.3 noise scale.

**Bid:** An informed seller hits the bid whenever settlement is below it. Balancing noise-trader profit (bid below 5.6, more likely to fill when higher) against informed losses gives a maximum near 4.3 (4.4 is nearly equal).

{"bid": 4.3, "ask": 6.6}

**Fair value:** Two heads so far, so the posterior on "always heads" is 0.8 and on "fair" is 0.2. Expected total heads = 0.8·6 + 0.2·4 = **5.6**.

**Ask:** The settlement value can't exceed 6, so an informed buyer never wants to buy at 6.0. Only noise buyers can take it, and any fill there earns about 0.4 in expectation.

**Bid:** Informed sellers arrive when the value is below the bid. A bid near 4.3 keeps that adverse selection modest while still earning a positive expected edge from noise sellers. My rough calculation puts the expected profit from this bid at about 0.09.

{"bid": 4.3, "ask": 6.0}

**Posterior and fair value:** Two heads so far gives P(biased coin | HH) = 0.8 and P(fair | HH) = 0.2. Settlement is 2 + (heads in flips 3–6). If the coin is biased, settlement is 6 for certain. If fair, it is 2 + Binomial(4, 0.5). So the public fair value is 0.2·4 + 0.8·6 = **5.6**, and settlement is at most 6.

**Ask:** Informed traders buy only when settlement exceeds my ask, and settlement never exceeds 6. An ask of 6.6 therefore gets no informed buys. Against noise traders, who buy when their valuation (5.6 ± 1.3) exceeds my ask, 6.6 maximises expected profit per quote.

**Bid:** Informed traders sell to me when settlement is below my bid. Weighing noise-seller profit against that adverse selection, the expected profit peaks around a bid of 4.3.

This matches my quote 4 and is slightly wider than quote 5 on the ask side. Position is 0, so both sides are available.

{"bid": 4.3, "ask": 6.6}

**Posterior:** Four heads in a row gives a likelihood of 1/16 under the fair coin and 1 under the always-heads coin. So P(always-heads) = 16/17 and P(fair) = 1/17. The settlement is 4 + (heads in flips 5 and 6), which is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029, and 4 with about 0.015. The public fair value is about 5.94.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only buys when the value (at most 6) is above my ask, so any ask at or above 6 avoids informed flow. Among those, noise-trader expected profit, 0.65 × P(valuation > A) × (A − 5.94), peaks near 6.9 (about 0.14).

**Bid:** Informed sellers only appear if the value is 4 or 5 (small probability), so the bid can sit close to fair value. Noise-trader expected profit, 0.65 × P(valuation < B) × (5.94 − B), peaks near 4.9–5.0. I'm choosing 4.9 because it's slightly better after the small informed-sell cost.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

Posterior after four heads: the coin is always-heads with probability 16/17, so the expected total is about 5.94. Settlement is 4 + (flips 5 and 6), so it can only be 4, 5 or 6, and a quote above 6 gets no informed buyers. Quoting bid 4.9 and ask 6.9 keeps adverse selection small on both sides while still capturing noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

**Posterior after flips 1-4 (all heads):**
- P(always-heads coin) = (1/2)(1) / [(1/2)(1) + (1/2)(1/16)] = 16/17 ≈ 0.941. P(fair coin) = 1/17.
- Public fair value = 4 + 2 × (16/17 + (1/17)(1/2)) = 4 + 33/17 ≈ **5.94**.
- Settlement distribution: S = 6 w.p. 65/68, S = 5 w.p. 2/68, S = 4 w.p. 1/68.

**Quote analysis.** The informed trader only trades when S is outside the quote, so it can never buy at an ask of 6.0 or more, and it only sells to us at a bid above 4. Expected gain per side, with noise traders at N(5.94, 1.3²):
- **Ask a:** gain = 0.65 × P(val > a) × (a − 5.94). This peaks near a = 6.9 (≈ 0.144). At 7.0 it is ≈ 0.143, at 6.8 ≈ 0.142.
- **Bid b:** gain = 0.65 × P(val < b) × (5.94 − b) − 0.35 × (informed S=4 or 5 losses). This peaks near b = 4.9 (≈ 0.139). At 5.0 it is ≈ 0.138, at 4.8 ≈ 0.137.

Each side's trade is determined by its own threshold and only one counterparty arrives, so the two sides add. Quoting bid 4.9 and ask 6.9 maximises the expected profit.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.9}

info.raw:
Before any reveals, the public fair value is E[heads] = 6 × E[p] = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5. Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.508, so an informed buyer would only buy at an ask below 6, and it can never be above 6.

- **Ask:** At 6.0 an informed buyer never trades, since V ≤ 6. A noise buyer trades with probability about 0.19 at a 1.5 markup over 4.5, for an expected gain of about 0.18. Lower asks give slightly less once informed adverse selection is counted.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers trade when V < bid. The expected net is roughly flat at bids of 2.7 to 2.8, at about 0.10 per quote. I'm choosing 2.7.

This ignores inventory risk, which is small at this stage.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

The coin must be fair: flip 2 was tails, which a heads-only coin cannot produce. The two earlier sales at my bids (2.7 and 2.5) were more likely from informed buyers when the settlement value was low, so the posterior on the settlement value moves down. Settlement is S = 1 + k, where k is the number of heads in flips 3 to 6. Weighting the prior by the sale likelihoods gives a posterior mean of about 2.04 for S, with P(S=2) ≈ 0.69.

Using a public fair value of 2.04 for noise traders (σ = 1.7) and this posterior for informed traders, expected profit per arrival is maximised near:
- Bid 0.8: no informed seller is possible below S = 1, and the noise-seller edge is about 0.19.
- Ask 3.5: the informed-buyer loss (S = 4 or 5) is small, and the noise-buyer edge is about 0.19.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 3.5}

**Reasoning (brief):**

- Flip 2 was tails, so the two-headed coin is ruled out. The coin is fair.
- Flips 1 and 2 give 1 head and 0 tails. Flips 3 to 6 are fair coin flips, so H = 1 + Bin(4, 0.5).
- The two early sales at my bids (2.7 and 2.5) and the no-trade at quote 3 shift the posterior toward fewer heads. Approximate posterior: P(H=1) ≈ 0.19, P(H=2) ≈ 0.75, P(H=3) ≈ 0.04, P(H=4) ≈ 0.015, P(H=5) ≈ 0.004. Public fair value m ≈ 1.9.
- Noise traders value the contract at about N(1.9, 1.7). Informed traders trade only when H is outside the quoted range.
- Expected gain on each side, with the informed-trader adverse selection included:
  - Ask: about 0.18 at 3.2, which is near the maximum. Informed buyers only appear when H ≥ 4.
  - Bid: about 0.19 at 0.6. Informed sellers would need H < 0.6, which is impossible.
- I am already long 2, so the bid side is the riskier one to add to, but the expected value still favours it. Both prices are valid multiples of 0.1, and bid ≤ ask.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.2}

The coin must be fair. Flip 2 was tails, which rules out the always-heads coin, so each remaining flip is heads with probability 0.5. The settlement value is S = 1 + X, where X is the number of heads in flips 5 and 6: S = 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5, 0.25. The public fair value is 2.

Noise traders value the contract around N(2, 1.7²). Informed traders know S. My position is +2 and does not affect the optimal quotes, because each trade's profit is simply price minus S.

- **Ask:** the expected contribution of selling at ask a is 0.35·E[(a−S)·1{S>a}] + 0.65·(a−2)·P(N>a). This is roughly 0.188 at a = 3.3, and it is near its maximum there. Above 3, informed buyers are gone, and the noise term peaks around 3.2–3.3.
- **Bid:** the expected contribution of buying at bid b is 0.35·E[(S−b)·1{S<b}] + 0.65·(2−b)·P(N<b). This is roughly 0.188 at b = 0.7, and it is near its maximum there. Above 1, informed sellers appear, which lowers the value.

Both sides are close to optimal, so I quote bid 0.7 and ask 3.3.

info.raw:

**Adverse selection:** An informed buyer takes my ask only when V > ask, and an informed seller takes my bid only when V < bid. Noise traders trade when their valuation (48.8 + N(0, 26)) crosses my price. For each candidate price I compared the expected profit from the noise flow against the expected loss to informed flow, using the distribution of H.

- **Ask:** The informed buyer can never profitably buy at 80, since V ≤ 80. At ask 80, only noise traders can buy (probability about 0.115 per quote), and the expected profit is about +2.3. Asks at 79 and 81 are slightly worse.
- **Bid:** The best bid is around 20, where the expected profit is about +2.0. Bids at 19 and 21 are slightly worse.

Under the prior, P(heads) = 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61, so the fair value is 8 × 0.61 × 10 = 48.8. A rough expected-profit check puts the best ask near 80 and the best bid near 18 to 20. Nothing has been revealed yet, so the fair value is unchanged from quote 1 and I'll keep the same quotes.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 80}

**Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask whenever the settlement exceeds it, so the ask has to sit above the fair value. Balancing the noise-trader profit against the informed-trader loss, the best ask is about 43. Settlement above 43 requires 5 or more total heads, which has about 1.7% probability.

**Bid:** Settlement is never below 10, so informed sellers cannot hit a bid under 10. The best bid is therefore where the noise-trader profit peaks, about 3.4, which rounds down to 3.

Both quotes are far from the fair value, but the previous 20/80 quotes earned almost nothing in expectation, and these should earn more.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 43}

**Fair value:** Flips 1–6 show 2 heads, and flips 7–8 are unknown. Updating on the 2 heads in 6 flips gives a posterior of about 0.80 / 0.19 / 0.004 over the coins (p = 0.3 / 0.4 / 0.9). The expected heads in flips 7–8 is about 0.64, so the public fair value is about 10 × (2 + 0.64) ≈ 26.4. Settlement is one of 20, 30 or 40 (probabilities about 0.46, 0.43, 0.11).

**Adverse selection:** Informed buyers (35%) buy only when V > ask, and informed sellers only when V < bid. Quoting an ask above 40 means no informed buyer will ever take it, and a bid at or below 20 means no informed seller will. The only trades I can then get are from noise traders, whose valuations are independent of V. Quoting near 26 would mostly trade with informed flow and lose money.

**Optimisation:** The expected profit on the ask side is (A − 26.4) × P(noise valuation > A), which is maximised near A = 46 (about 2.87 per quote). By symmetry the bid side is maximised near B = 7 (about 2.87). Neither trade reveals any coin information, since a trade at 46 or 7 can only come from a noise trader, so the fair value doesn't shift before quote 6.

Nothing has been revealed yet, so the public fair value is the prior expectation. **Fair value:** P(heads on each remaining flip) ≈ 0.689, so E[heads] ≈ 2 + 6(0.689) ≈ 6.135 and the public fair value is about 5 × 6.135 ≈ **30.7**. Settlement takes values 10, 15, …, 40, with mass concentrated around 30–35.

**Quote 4 (bid 2.0, ask 5.0)**

- **Settlement distribution:** Since the settlement is an integer, V = 1 + Binomial(5, p) mixed over the posterior gives P(V=1..6) ≈ (0.063, 0.213, 0.321, 0.264, 0.116, 0.021).
- **Ask side:** An informed buyer takes the ask only when V exceeds it, so the ask must sit above the integer mass the informed traders can exploit. Expected profit per quote, at half weight for each counterparty type, peaks near 5.0 (about +0.065) and is negative for asks in the 3–4 range.
- **Bid side:** An informed seller hits the bid only when V is below it. Expected profit peaks at 2.0 (about +0.075), just below the jump in informed selling at V=2.

This is a one-quote myopic optimisation and ignores inventory and later quotes. The wide spread is driven by the integer settlement and the adverse-selection threshold, not by the fair value sitting in the middle.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.0}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 to 5 show 2 heads and 3 tails. The posterior on the coin is P(0.3) ≈ 0.19, P(0.4) ≈ 0.32, P(0.5) ≈ 0.49, so E[p] ≈ 0.43. Expected settlement is 2 + 0.43 ≈ 2.43.

**Adverse selection:** Settlement is 2 or 3 (flip 6 is the only unknown). An informed counterparty buys from us only if settlement is above our ask, and sells to us only if settlement is below our bid.
- A bid at or below 2 never meets an informed seller, so only noise traders can hit it.
- An ask at or above 3 never meets an informed buyer, so only noise traders can lift it.

**Quote:** Within those no-informed zones, each side's expected profit is (distance from 2.43) × P(noise trader crosses), which peaks at about 0.98 away from 2.43. That gives a bid near 1.45 and an ask near 3.4. Bids round down, so the bid is 1.4. The ask of 3.4 is already a multiple of 0.1.

{"bid": 1.4, "ask": 3.4}

**Posterior on the coin.** Flips 1–5 are H,T,T,T,H (2 heads, 3 tails). Weighting the prior by the likelihood gives P(p=0.3) ≈ 0.19, P(p=0.4) ≈ 0.32, P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.49. So P(flip 6 = heads) ≈ 0.429.

**Settlement and fair value.** Flips 1, 5 are heads and flips 2–4 are tails, so settlement S = 2 + flip 6. Fair value F = 2 + 0.429 ≈ 2.43.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer takes my ask only if S = 3, so any ask below 3 loses money to informed flow. At an ask of 3 or above, informed flow never trades. Above 3, the noise-trader term (A − F)·P(V > A) with V ~ N(2.43, 1.3²) peaks near A ≈ 3.4. Asks of 3.3–3.5 are almost equally good, and 3.4 is best among them.

**Bid side.** An informed seller hits my bid only if S = 2, so bids above 2 lose money to informed flow. Below 2, the noise-trader term (F − B)·P(V < B) peaks near B ≈ 1.45. Bids of 1.4 and 1.5 are essentially tied, and 1.5 is marginally better.

Both quotes are the best available given the posterior. Only this quote remains, so there is no later stage to consider.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 3.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The coin's bias is unknown, so the public fair value is the prior expectation. Each flip has heads probability 0.3(0.2) + 0.4(0.5) + 0.3(0.7) = 0.47, so 7 flips give an expected 3.29 heads. I'll quote symmetrically around 3.29: bid 3.2 (rounded down from 3.25 to a 0.1 multiple) and ask 3.4 (rounded up from 3.35).

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 3.4}

The prior mean for the coin's heads probability is 0.3(0.2) + 0.4(0.5) + 0.3(0.7) = 0.47, so the expected number of heads over 7 flips is 7 × 0.47 = 3.29. No flips are revealed yet, so nothing has changed since quote 1. I'll keep the same quotes around that fair value.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 3.4}

**Reasoning**

- **Prior fair value:** The mixture mean of the coin bias is 0.3(0.2) + 0.4(0.5) + 0.3(0.7) = 0.47, so the expected number of heads in 7 flips is about 3.29.
- **Update from the trade history:** Quote 2 sold to us at our bid of 3.2. An informed seller only sells when S < 3.2, and a noise seller sells when V < 3.2, which happens about 49% of the time. Weighting the settlement distribution by these likelihoods lowers the public fair value to about 2.97. Quote 1 had no trade, which is uninformative here because an informed trader always trades at integer S.
- **Adverse selection:** Tight quotes near 3 lose money on average, because informed traders (20%) pick off whichever side is wrong. Wide quotes earn a premium from noise traders (80%), whose valuations are centred on 2.97 with sd 2.7.
- **Optimisation (single-quote expected profit):** Maximising expected profit on each side gives an ask of about 5.2 and a bid of about 0.8–0.9. The bid is nearly flat between 0.8 and 0.9, so I take 0.8. Expected profit is roughly 0.35 from each side, and the position is unaffected.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 5.2}

Public fair value after flip 1 is about 3.9 (roughly 4.3 before the trade-history update). The quote 2 sell at 3.2 and the quote 3 no-trade slightly lower the estimate. Because the noise-trader spread is wide (sd 2.7) and informed trades are 20% likely, the profit-maximising quotes sit well away from fair value. A bid near 1.8 and an ask near 6.0 each give roughly 0.36 expected profit, while an ask near 4 is negative because informed buyers would likely take it.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 6.0}

**Fair value:** Flip 1 was heads, so the posterior over coin bias is about 0.13 (p=0.2), 0.43 (p=0.5), 0.45 (p=0.7). The expected bias is about 0.55, so the expected total heads is 1 + 6 × 0.55 ≈ 4.31.

**Position:** I'm long 1, so I'll skew slightly toward selling. I'm lowering the ask a little to attract buyers and keeping the bid modestly below fair value to limit further buying.

**Quote:** Bid 3.5 is about 0.8 below fair value and ask 5.0 is about 0.7 above it. Against informed traders, expected adverse loss on each side is roughly 0.06–0.07, while noise-trader spread capture is roughly 0.2 per side.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.0}

**Fair value.** Flips 1–3 are H, H, T. Flips 4–7 are unrevealed, so the posterior on the coin is:

- p=0.2: 0.0096 / 0.1037 ≈ 0.093
- p=0.5: 0.0500 / 0.1037 ≈ 0.482
- p=0.7: 0.0441 / 0.1037 ≈ 0.425

The posterior probability that a remaining flip is heads is ≈ 0.557. Expected settlement is 2 + 4(0.557) ≈ **4.23**.

**Quote.** A noise trader's valuation is N(4.23, 2.7²), and informed traders only trade when they are on the profitable side of my quote. I compute the expected profit per quote on each side (fill probability × margin, minus the adverse-selection loss from informed trades) and pick the quote that maximises it. Inventory (+2) doesn't change the expected value, so it doesn't shift the quote.

- Ask: the noise term peaks near 6.2–6.3 (≈0.367 expected profit). Informed buyers can't profitably lift an ask above the maximum settlement value of 6, so there is no adverse-selection cost there.
- Bid: the symmetric optimum is near 2.1 (≈0.365). The only adverse-selection cost is a small loss from an informed seller when settlement is 2.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 6.3}

**Fair value:** Flips 1 to 3 show 2 heads, and the posterior over the coin is roughly P(0.2)=0.09, P(0.5)=0.48, P(0.7)=0.43, so the posterior mean heads probability is about 0.557. The four unrevealed flips (4 to 7) are expected to give about 2.23 heads, so the expected settlement is about 2 + 2.23 ≈ 4.23.

**Ask choice:** Settlement S = 2 + (heads in flips 4 to 7) can be at most 6. An informed buyer only hits my ask when S > ask, so any ask at or above 6 avoids informed flow entirely. Noise buyers hit the ask with probability P(N(4.23, 2.7) > ask). Expected profit per quote peaks near an ask of 6.2 to 6.3, at about 0.37 each. The two are essentially tied, so I'll use 6.3.

**Bid:** Pulled at position +3, so null.

{"bid": null, "ask": 6.3}

**Fair value:** The public revealed flips are 3 heads in 5. The posterior on the coin is about 0.066 for p=0.2, 0.537 for p=0.5, and 0.398 for p=0.7. That gives E[p] ≈ 0.56, so the expected settlement is 3 + 2(0.56) ≈ 4.12. Settlement can only be 3, 4 or 5, with probabilities about 0.21, 0.46 and 0.33.

**Adverse selection:** Because settlement is at most 5, an informed buyer would never take an ask of 6.1, and an informed seller would never take a bid of 2.0. So the informed side costs nothing at these prices.

**Noise-trader edge:** Noise valuations are roughly N(4.12, 2.7). Expected profit per side is maximised near a bid of 2.0–2.1 and an ask of 6.0–6.2, at about 0.37 per quote on each side. I'm quoting 2.0 and 6.1.

**Position:** Inventory doesn't change expected profit, and I'm at +2. A bid of 2.0 can take me to +3, which is within limits.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 6.1}

**Posterior after flips 1–5:** The revealed flips are 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, so there are 3 heads in 5 flips. The coin posterior is roughly 0.07 for p=0.2, 0.54 for p=0.5 and 0.40 for p=0.7, giving E[p] ≈ 0.56.

**Settlement distribution:** Settlement S = 3 + H, where H is the number of heads in flips 6–7. Then P(S=3) ≈ 0.21, P(S=4) ≈ 0.46, P(S=5) ≈ 0.33, and E[S] ≈ 4.12. This is the public fair value μ for noise traders, who have σ = 2.7.

**Bid:** Informed sellers hit the bid only when S < B. Since S ≥ 3, a bid of 2.1 gives zero adverse selection. Noise sellers arrive with probability 0.8·Φ((B−μ)/σ), and the expected profit per side is 0.8·Φ((B−μ)/σ)·(μ−B). This is maximised near B ≈ 2.1 (about 0.367 expected profit).

**Ask:** Informed buyers lift the ask only when S > A. At A = 6.2 they can never trade, since S ≤ 5. Noise buyers arrive with probability 0.8·(1−Φ((A−μ)/σ)), and the expected profit is 0.8·(1−Φ((A−μ)/σ))·(A−μ). This peaks around A ≈ 6.15, so 6.2 is the best 0.1-rounded ask (about 0.367 expected profit, essentially tied with 6.1).

Both sides are chosen to maximise expected settlement profit, since this is the last quote.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 6.2}

The fair value is 10 × 7 × 0.62 = 43.4, since the coin is 0.5 with probability 0.4 and 0.7 with probability 0.6. Nothing has been revealed, so the fair value hasn't changed. My estimate of the trade-off between noise and informed flow puts the best ask near 56 and the best bid near 31, so I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 30.9, "ask": 55.9}

Posterior after flips 1 to 3 (two heads in three): P(coin p=0.7) ≈ 0.64, so the expected heads per remaining flip is about 0.63. The public fair value is about 10 × (2 + 4 × 0.63) ≈ 45.1, and the spread is wide because of adverse selection from informed traders. I'm short 1 unit, so I'll skew the quotes up to make buying back more likely.

{"bid": 42.0, "ask": 49.5}

**Fair value:** After flips 1–3 (one tail, two heads), the posterior on the 0.7 coin is 0.638. Expected p is 0.628, so expected total heads is 2 + 4(0.628) ≈ 4.51, and the public fair value is about 45.1.

**Settlement distribution:** Heads in flips 4–7 are a mixture of Bin(4, 0.5) and Bin(4, 0.7). Settlement V = 10·(2 + X) takes values 20 to 60, with P(V=50) ≈ 0.35 and P(V=60) ≈ 0.18.

**Ask:** Informed buyers take the ask only when V > ask, so they mainly hit us at 50 or 60. Noise buyers take it when their valuation (about N(45.1, 11)) exceeds the ask. Maximising the expected profit per ask gives an optimum near 57, with an expected profit of about 0.90.

**Bid:** By symmetry, informed sellers hit us only when V < bid, mainly at 20 or 30. Noise sellers hit it when their valuation is below the bid. Maximising gives an optimum near 34, with an expected profit of about 0.80.

Only one counterparty arrives and the two sides are mutually exclusive, so the per-side profits add. The objective is expected profit at settlement, so I'm not adding an inventory penalty for the current short position of -2.

{"bid": 34.0, "ask": 57.0}

Fair value is about 49.3, from the posterior after flips 1-4 (3 heads in 4 flips, so P(fair coin) ≈ 0.29). Settlement can only be 30, 40, 50 or 60, with probabilities of roughly 0.06, 0.24, 0.42 and 0.28.

Quoting around fair value would hand informed traders the 60 outcome cheaply, so I widen the quote to the points where each side's expected edge from noise traders is highest, net of informed losses:
- **Ask at 60:** informed buyers never trade (60 is not above 60), and noise buyers still pay well above fair value.
- **Bid at 40:** informed sellers only hit us at 30, and noise sellers at 40 still give a positive edge.

Being short 2 doesn't change the expected value at fair, so inventory isn't a factor here.

{"bid": 40.0, "ask": 60.0}

**Posterior on the coin:** Flips 1-4 show three heads and one tail. The likelihoods are 0.25 for the fair coin and 0.4116 for the 0.7 coin, so P(fair) ≈ 0.29 and P(0.7) ≈ 0.71.

**Settlement distribution:** Three heads are already known. The remaining flips 5-7 give k heads with probabilities k=0: 0.055, k=1: 0.243, k=2: 0.422, k=3: 0.280. So the settlement value is V ∈ {30, 40, 50, 60}, with public fair value E[V] ≈ 49.3.

**Ask:** The informed trader buys only when V > ask, and noise buyers arrive with probability depending on the ask. The expected profit from selling at ask A is maximised near A = 60 (about 1.15 per quote, versus about 1.09 at 59 or 61).

**Bid:** The informed trader sells only when V < bid, and noise sellers depend on the bid. The expected profit from buying at bid B is maximised near B = 40 (about 1.01, flat between 39 and 41).

Position is -2, well within limits, and the objective is linear in value, so inventory does not change the optimal quotes.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 60}

**Reasoning**

- **Posterior on the coin:** Flips 2–6 are all heads and flip 1 is tails, so the observed sequence is 5 heads and 1 tail. Fair coin: 0.4 × 0.5⁶ ≈ 0.00625. Biased coin: 0.6 × 0.7⁵ × 0.3 ≈ 0.03025. So P(fair) ≈ 0.17 and P(biased) ≈ 0.83.
- **Flip 7:** P(heads) ≈ 0.17 × 0.5 + 0.83 × 0.7 ≈ 0.666. Expected total heads ≈ 5.67, so the public fair value is about 56.7.
- **Informed traders:** The settlement value is either 50 or 60. An informed buyer never buys at an ask above 60, and an informed seller never sells at a bid of 50 or below. So quoting an ask above 60 and a bid at or below 50 avoids adverse selection entirely.
- **Ask:** Against noise traders with valuations around N(56.7, 11), the expected profit per quote is maximised near an ask of about 65. Sales at that price are profitable in expectation, since 65 is well above the fair value.
- **Bid:** The same logic on the buy side gives a bid of about 48.4, which keeps the bid below the informed-seller threshold.
- **Inventory:** At −3 the position is within limits either way. Settlement is linear, so inventory doesn't change the expected-profit calculation for this quote.

{"bid": 48.4, "ask": 65.0}

**Posterior on the coin:** Flips 1 to 6 show 5 heads in 6. The fair coin (prior 2/5) has likelihood proportional to 0.0375 and the 0.7 coin (prior 3/5) to 0.1815, so P(0.7 coin) ≈ 0.83. That gives P(flip 7 = heads) ≈ 0.666.

**Settlement:** Total heads is 5 + flip 7, so the settlement is 60 with probability ≈ 0.666 and 50 with probability ≈ 0.334. The public fair value is about 56.66.

**Ask side:** Informed buyers only take the ask when the value is above it, so an ask at or above 60 gets no informed trades. Noise traders (mean 56.66, SD 11) buy when their valuation exceeds the ask. Expected profit peaks near an ask of about 65, worth roughly +1.2.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers only hit the bid when the value is below it, so a bid at or below 50 gets no informed trades. Noise traders sell when their valuation is below the bid. Expected profit peaks near a bid of about 48.4, worth roughly +1.2.

Both sides are independent events for a single counterparty, so the quotes add. Position −3 is within limits for one more trade in either direction.

info.raw:
No flips are revealed yet. Under the prior, P(0.7 coin) = 0.6, so expected heads = 7 × 0.62 = 4.34 and the public fair value is about 43.4. Quote 1 produced no trade, which is informative: an informed buyer would have hit an ask of 57 if V > 57, and an informed seller would have hit a bid of 30 if V < 30. Conditioning on that, the fair value falls to about 42.7, and the distribution thins out at the tails.

Re-optimising against the updated distribution (noise traders with sd 11, 35% informed):
- **Bid:** The expected-profit optimum sits at the discrete kink at 30, so 30 stays.
- **Ask:** The optimum moves down from about 57 to about 54, since the probability that an informed buyer arrives has fallen. Rounding up gives 53.8.

{"bid": 30, "ask": 53.8}

**Fair value:** Three heads are revealed, so the posterior is P(fair coin) ≈ 0.196 and P(70% coin) ≈ 0.804. The expected heads in the remaining four flips is about 2.64, so the expected settlement is about 56.4.

**Settlement distribution:** Settlement is 10 × (3 + heads in flips 4–7), so it takes values 30, 40, 50, 60 or 70 with probabilities of about 0.02, 0.11, 0.29, 0.38 and 0.21.

**Adverse selection:** Informed buyers appear only when settlement exceeds my ask, and informed sellers only when it falls below my bid. Noise traders carry no information beyond the fair value. For each candidate price I computed the expected profit per side, E[(ask − V) · 1{buy}] or E[(V − bid) · 1{sell}], given the probability of each counterparty type trading.

- **Ask:** profit peaks around 69–70 (about 0.96 per side). Asking 57 loses money, since buyers at that price have expected value near 59.
- **Bid:** profit peaks around 45–46 (about 0.83). Bidding 50 or higher is worse.

The distribution is skewed toward 60, which is why the ask sits further from fair value than the bid.

{"bid": 46, "ask": 69}

Four heads so far (flips 1-4), and the prior is 2/5 fair and 3/5 biased to 0.7. The posterior is about 0.15 fair and 0.85 biased. Flips 5-7 are still unknown, so the expected total is about 6.0 heads and the fair value is about 60.1.

The settlement value takes one of four values, with approximate probabilities:
- 40: 0.04
- 50: 0.22
- 60: 0.43
- 70: 0.31

Informed traders (35%) buy from me only when the settlement value is above my ask, and sell to me only when it is below my bid. Noise traders (65%) trade based on fair value plus N(0, 11) noise.

Ask: at 70, informed traders can never buy profitably because the value cannot exceed 70. The noise-trader edge there is about 1.19 in expectation, which beats nearby asks such as 69 or 71.

Bid: at 50, informed traders sell to me only in the 40-value state. The expected edge is about 1.03, which beats 49 or 51.

The expected edge per quote is about 2.2. This is a myopic one-quote optimum and ignores inventory effects from future quotes.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 70}

The fair value is about 61.5 after updating on the trade history. Here are the key steps:

- **Coin posterior from the revealed flips:** four heads so far gives P(coin = 0.7) ≈ 0.85. The remaining flips (5, 6, 7) imply a settlement distribution over {40, 50, 60, 70}.
- **Trade-history update:** the earlier trades (sold to us at 46, bought from us at 69) and the no-trade result at 50/70 shift the posterior toward 70. The approximate posterior is 40: 9%, 50: 22%, 60: 14%, 70: 55%.
- **Bid:** maximising expected profit from a sale to us gives a bid of 50. A bid of 51 or higher adds more informed-seller losses than it gains in noise-trader fills.
- **Ask:** the informed buyer only buys when the value is strictly above the ask, so an ask of 70 avoids the most likely settlement value. Asks of 69.9 or below, or 71 or above, both give lower expected profit.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 70}

Six heads are revealed, so the posterior is about 92% on the 0.7 coin. That gives P(flip 7 = heads) ≈ 0.684 and a public fair value of about 66.84. Settlement is 60 or 70, depending on flip 7.

Both sides should use the noise-trader optimum, since the informed trader only trades profitably against a quote inside its range:

- **Ask:** At 70 or above, the informed trader never buys. The noise-trader optimum is about 66.84 + 0.75 × 11 ≈ 75.1, which beats quoting inside 60–70.
- **Bid:** Quoting at or below 60 means the informed trader never sells to me. The noise-trader optimum is about 66.84 − 0.75 × 11 ≈ 58.6, which rounds down to 58.5.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 7/10, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
